citation.title: AI support for ethical decision-making around resuscitation: proceed with care
citation.venue: medRxiv, version 1 posted 19 August 2020; related journal version online 2021, print 2022

reading.source_scope_note: Eleven exploratory clinician interviews plus a proposed ethical framework, with no trained AI system, predictive validation, clinical trial or patient-outcome estimate. Graph 1 and Boxes 1–3 cited in the text are absent from this 14-page supplied preprint; detailed interview results and use-case illustrations therefore remain incompletely accessible.
access_limits: All supplied pages read, but the cross-referenced graph and three boxes are not present as text, images or substantive vector figures. Do not reconstruct their themes, quotes or scenarios from surrounding prose.
Interview guide, original German transcripts, English summaries and translated key quotations are not supplied; the guide is offered on request. No author contact was made.
The related journal article and missing public full-page content were not retrieved after 403 responses. Version identity does not authorize copying later claims into this preprint review.

No EHR dataset, patient-preference dataset, trained code-status model, evaluation code or raw participant data reviewed. Cited original trials, reviews, legal sources and psychology papers are not independently read merely by appearing in the bibliography.

study.sample: Summer 2019, one Swiss university hospital: 11 voluntary semi-structured interviews, seven physicians and four nurses, six women and five men. Maximum-variation selection covers emergency care, internal medicine, intensive care, surgery and palliative care, with differing seniority. Interviews lasted 25–45 minutes, in German, recorded and transcribed. No recruitment denominator or refusal count reported.
study.analysis: Expert-interview analysis is cited, but the supplied narrative does not specify coder count, complete codebook, disagreement process, saturation assessment or reflexivity. Missing Boxes 1–2 constrain inspection of themes and supporting excerpts. Absence of these details here does not prove the team never used them.
study.ethics: Relevant IRB approval and informed consent for recorded interviews are stated. No approval date/identifier is supplied; do not invent one or allege no approval.
study.institutional_context: Approximately 120,000 documented resuscitation decisions and EHR code-status recording since 2013 describe a potential future training site, not 120,000 analyzed patients or valid preference labels. The selected institution already offers advance-care planning and some clinician training; it is not a representative hospital sample.
study.results_boundary: The narrative reports clinician awareness of documentation challenges and general openness to considering AI support. No participant-level acceptance rate, representative prevalence, quantitative effect, tested psychological mechanism or implementation success is given. Brainstormed strengths/limitations are not evaluations of an operational product.
study.proposed_role: A consultative tool could prompt conversations, offer a second opinion or assist deliberation when a patient cannot communicate. Authors explicitly deny decisional authority and say it should never replace conversations with patients, legal representatives or the treatment team. These are proposed safeguards, not empirically demonstrated effects.
study.prediction_targets: Authors distinguish patient-preference prediction from predicted resuscitation outcomes and sketch combining them. The model is hypothetical: no algorithm, feature selection, training cohort, calibration, error rate, external validation, subgroup assessment or outcome improvement is supplied.
study.label_validity: Whether CPR occurred or a code status was recorded may reflect clinicians, emergencies, institutional routines or earlier process flaws rather than informed patient preferences. Authors warn against these accessible surrogate labels and favor well-elicited preferences. Similarity to other patients does not establish this individual’s wishes or consent.
study.dynamic_preferences: Outcome-dependent preferences and later code-status updates are proposed, not measured. Different views can be coherent or change with circumstances; do not treat uncertainty as proof that the system knows the patient’s authentic values.
study.implementation: Explainability, access management, bias monitoring, user training and communication safeguards are framework recommendations. Explainability may affect acceptance but has not been experimentally tested here. Trust, accuracy, fairness, authorization and patient participation need separate evaluation.
study.avoidance_risk: The paper warns that clinicians might substitute predictions for difficult conversations or outsource a core task. It does not measure conversational avoidance, experiential avoidance, actual authority delegation or professional deskilling.
study.normative_limits: Claims that well-designed support can make immediate significant impact and that machine predictions may become more authoritative are prospective expectations. High-risk clinical adoption, a duty to use AI, valid DNAR decisions and current legal standards are not established by this pilot. DNAR is a resuscitation-specific status, not a blanket refusal of treatment.

summary: No new terms. Add a clearly labeled qualitative/framework citation to shared decision-making, algorithmic authority and perceived explainability; preserve non-counting boundaries concerning consultation versus delegation, proxy labels versus value misgeneralisation, and dialogue avoidance. Correct the file/version attribution and disclose absent graph/boxes instead of inventing detailed interview findings.

findings.definition: An approach in which the person affected and the relevant professional participate together in choosing a course of action.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing construct; this qualitative pilot and ethical framework add context or a boundary, not a distinct behavior definition.

evidence.quote: in accordance with best practice principles of shared decision-making

findings.evidence_scope: The framework recommends integrating predictions into communication with patients, relatives and staff and training users in shared decision-making. Eleven clinician interviews motivate the proposal; no shared-decision intervention or patient outcome is tested.
findings.boundary: Predicted preferences are not expressed consent. Participation, capacity, valid representation and the affected person’s actual values must be assessed separately; a tool cannot replace conversation merely because it predicts a likely preference.

findings.definition: Treating an algorithmic system as a credible or legitimate source for deciding what information to accept or how to act.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing construct; this qualitative pilot and ethical framework add context or a boundary, not a distinct behavior definition.

evidence.quote: It does not have decisional authority and should never replace

findings.evidence_scope: The paper distinguishes a consultative second opinion from decisional authority and anticipates a possible future shift in epistemic authority. This is a role/governance argument, not a measured authority-transfer effect.
findings.boundary: Predictive accuracy does not automatically confer permission to decide, a current legal duty to obey, or knowledge of an individual’s preferences. Future capability and clinician openness do not establish safe deployment.

findings.definition: A person’s judgment that a system’s operation or recommendations are understandable and can be explained.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing construct; this qualitative pilot and ethical framework add context or a boundary, not a distinct behavior definition.

evidence.quote: include elements of explanations from social sciences [38].

findings.evidence_scope: Explainability is proposed as a design requirement for acceptance and trust in sensitive preference-related decisions. No explanation manipulation, comprehension measure or causal trust effect is supplied.
findings.boundary: An understandable story need not be faithful, accurate or adequate for consent. Explainability is not interchangeable with actual reliability, accountability or patient participation; acceptance should not be maximized independently of warranted trust.

findings.definition: Transferring decision-making authority to another party who chooses on one's behalf.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing construct; this qualitative pilot and ethical framework add context or a boundary, not a distinct behavior definition.

evidence.quote: the AI system would be conceived to play a consultative rather than a prescriptive role,

findings.evidence_scope: The proposed system advises patients/proxies/clinicians while retaining human decision-making. The paper warns against outsourcing the core task, rather than reporting that participants delegated actual choices.
findings.boundary: Advice, predicted preferences, execution and transfer of decisional authority are distinct. No observed delegation rate or transfer of accountability is established; this is a non-counting boundary.

findings.definition: Learning a proxy for the intended value and applying it off-distribution.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing construct; this qualitative pilot and ethical framework add context or a boundary, not a distinct behavior definition.

evidence.quote: they may not reflect patients’ wishes.

findings.evidence_scope: The framework warns that recorded CPR treatment or code status can be an unsuitable label for informed patient preferences. It supplies a target-validity concern before training, not an observed generalization failure.
findings.boundary: A mislabeled training target differs from learning a proxy and applying it off-distribution. No trained model, distribution shift or observed value failure is reported. Do not call the proposed preference predictor reward hacking or infer a successful manipulation.

findings.definition: Guessing at an ambiguous request and answering, instead of asking the clarifying question that would resolve it.
findings.novelty_rationale: Existing construct; this qualitative pilot and ethical framework add context or a boundary, not a distinct behavior definition.

evidence.quote: tendencies to avoid difficult conversations with patients or family members about DNAR status by

findings.evidence_scope: The procedural framework warns about replacing a difficult patient/family conversation with algorithmic prediction. This is a prospective communication risk; it is not measured in the eleven interviews as an established behavioral effect.
findings.boundary: Clinician conversation avoidance is not identical to an AI guessing an ambiguous task. Patient incapacity or emergency constraints can legitimately limit questioning, and no subjective avoidance motive or actual loss of consent is demonstrated.

source_corrections.location: PDF page 6, description of interview questions
source_corrections.reported: The decision to attempt resuscitation (DNAR) or not.
source_corrections.correction: DNAR expands to Do Not Attempt to Resuscitate, as correctly stated in the abstract. The parenthetical placement in the methods is misleading; distinguish a decision about resuscitation status from a DNAR order specifically.
source_corrections.scope: Internal terminology clarification, not clinical or legal advice.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: Graph 1 and Boxes 1–3 are cross-referenced but absent from this 14-page file. Their detailed pathways, themes, quotations and use cases cannot be treated as reviewed. Public-page 403 responses do not prove the material is absent from every version.

Country X remains an editorial placeholder, although the methods name a Swiss university hospital and discuss University Hospital Zurich material. Retain the reported setting; do not infer a different country or hidden fabricated study.

The peer-reviewed imaging meta-analysis and an overlapping author/title SSRN report may be related versions. Bibliographic proximity is insufficient to treat them as independent corroborating studies; neither was independently fully reviewed here.

unresolved_source_discrepancies.location: PDF pages 2 and 11, capability and impact expectations
unresolved_source_discrepancies.finding: Broad statements about reliably predicting imminent clinical events, replacing expert work or immediate practical impact are secondary/prospective claims. They are not validated by the qualitative pilot and cannot support current clinical deployment without task-specific source review.

methodological_limits: Small, purposefully selected single-center professional sample; no patient or surrogate interviews, representative acceptance estimate or measured care outcome.
Absent results boxes and limited coding detail restrict appraisal of the qualitative evidence. Do not convert thematic openness into a prevalence claim.
No AI system trained or prospectively evaluated. Institutional record counts do not establish preference-label validity or benefits.
Proposed explainability, communication and monitoring safeguards are not causal intervention evidence. Clinical and legal judgments require evidence beyond this historical preprint.

cross_paper_learning.finding: Both concern healthcare attitudes rather than verified clinical outcomes. This paper’s 11 interviews and framework are not a quantitative replication of the ophthalmology survey or evidence resolving its conflicting surgery tables.

Perceived impartiality and public support for fictional prioritization do not establish patient-specific values. This framework highlights the separate need for preference elicitation, suitable targets and meaningful participation.
As in the live-action progress report, planned methods and anticipated benefits must remain distinct from completed analysis. Here interviews were completed, but the AI predictor remains a proposal.

deferred.term: Values clarification / advance care planning / substituted judgment
deferred.reason: Relevant decision practices are mentioned or motivated, but the source does not provide a sufficiently distinct named behavior definition or reviewed original method here. Read the original referenced methods before creating further entries.
A secondary statement about relatives’ decisions is not a new defined mechanism; projection, incomplete knowledge, differing values and decision framing are not separated.
Prospective risk, overlapping existing clarification avoidance and decision delegation; no independently demonstrated new process.

limitations: No new entries, independent final-version paper credit, timeline series, patient-consent inference, automatic ethical/harm edges or clinical advice.
